chapter_theme: Continuing the sermon on the four states of birth, the sage Munichandran describes the five-sensed animals, the five kinds of humans (of the land of enjoyment, of the islands, the divine, the beastlike, and those of the land of deeds, who alone can reach bliss by penance), the five classes of gods, and then, in short lines, the endless pains of hell, where bodies rejoin like water, old enemies fight and killing and flesh-eating are punished in fire; midway he hints to Neelakesi that her own kin are among the demon gods, and she agrees to keep listening.

cast.role: the Jain sage whose penance Neelakesi cannot break and who preaches the dharma to her
the demoness of the burning-ground temple, here in the form of a princess, listening to the sermon

80.reading: The sage lists the five-sensed animals, those with many legs, eight, and fewer pair by pair, the flyers, walkers, crawlers and creepers, which have hearing as the fifth sense and fill the sea and the islands.
80.nuance: The verse sorts animals as a Jain classification does, by the number of senses (இந்தியம் ஐந்து) and by legs and gait, not by use to man; the count of legs falls 'two by two' (இரண்டிரண்டே இழிந்த) from eight.

claims.claim: animals with all five senses, hearing the last, are many in kind by legs and gait and fill sea and islands

81.reading: Animals are born from wombs of mixed heat and cold, from membranes, eggs and sprouting, cannot act on what they are told, consume the fruit of the deeds they did, and wander taking one body after another, like and unlike.
81.nuance: Line 2 (செப்புவ செப்பில் செய்கைகள் ஆற்றம்) is hard to divide: it may say the animals cannot do what they are told, or that they cannot do the deeds that would free them; the reading is not fixed. போர்த்தும், பொடித்தும், பொரித்தும் seem to name the modes of birth (in a membrane, by sprouting, by hatching).

claims.claim: animals arise by several modes of birth and wander from body to body consuming the fruit of their own deeds

82.reading: Asked to tell the kinds of humans, the sage names five, the good, the bad, the divine, the base humans and the rest, and says the first of them dwell in the great land of enjoyment.
82.nuance: சொல்லுக தன்மை என்பாய் எனில் (if you say, tell their nature) shows the sermon as answers to the listener's questions, though she has asked nothing aloud in these verses. The land of enjoyment (போகப் பெருநிலம்) is where pleasure comes without labour; the sage does not praise it, and 86 will place release in the land of deeds instead.

claims.claim: humans are of five kinds, and the first kind live in a land of enjoyment

83.reading: The bad humans live in the small lands of the islands, faulty and lacking in qualities from their kings down, and even if they hold to great penance they do not reach the higher state; so the sage tells the doe-eyed woman.
83.nuance: The claim limits penance by birth: the same tapas that frees in 86 bears no such fruit here. தன்மை பெறார் may mean they do not gain the state penance gives, or do not gain good nature at all; the first fits the contrast with 86.

claims.claim: humans of the small island lands, wanting in qualities, do not attain the higher state even by great penance

84.reading: The divine humans are those who open the ford, those of heaped-up merit who bear the wheel and their companions, the sky-going Vidyadharas and the unfailing white ones, the sage tells the woman with fresh bangles.
84.nuance: தீர்த்தம் திறப்பவர் (those who open the ford) is the Tamil form of the Tirthankara title; ஆழியர் (wheel-bearers) are world-ruling kings. Who the ஐயவர் and வெள்ளியர் are, and what பப்பியர் in line 4 means, the verse alone does not settle.

claims.claim: the highest humans are the founders of the ford, the wheel-bearing kings and the sky-going Vidyadharas

85.reading: The base humans, ugly of form with tails, horns and curved teeth, live in the islands between and do not touch right conduct or right vision.
85.nuance: சீலமும் காட்சியும் (conduct and vision) are two of the Jain three jewels; their absence, not the beastlike form, is what makes these men low. The edition prints தீண்டலு ரந்தரத் where the sense needs தீண்டலர் அந்தரத்.

claims.claim: the base humans of the intermediate islands have beastlike forms and are untouched by right conduct and right vision

86.reading: Those called humans in the full sense are of the land of deeds, wooded and green, whose nature is that by penance their dark karma departs and they reach the highest bliss.
86.nuance: கரும நிலம் (land of deeds) is set against the land of enjoyment of 82: release is open only where people must act and can do penance. The name of the land in line 1 (ஆவிதையம்) is not clear and may be corrupt.

claims.claim: only humans of the land of deeds can shed their karma by penance and reach the highest bliss

87.reading: The gods are of five kinds, Bhavanas, Vyantaras, Jyotishkas, Kalpas and beyond them Vaimanikas, and in detail the first are ten with the fire-princes; the sage wonders whether telling more to the woman with flowered hair is unfitting.
87.nuance: The gods appear as one more class of births in the list that began with hell-beings and animals, ranked and numbered, not as objects of worship. The closing doubt (சொல்லல் பொல்லாது கொல்) prepares the turn in 88.

claims.claim: the gods are five classes of embodied beings, the Bhavana gods being ten in kind

88.reading: The sage names eight kinds of Vyantara gods, from the sweet-voiced ones to 'your own kin'; at that the woman suffers like wet ghee near fire, and when he says that her nature will be known later and she should hear dharma, she consents.
88.nuance: நுமர் ஈறா (ending with your kin) is the sage letting her know that he sees what she is: the last of the eight Vyantara classes are the demons, and she is a demoness in a princess's form. Lines 1 and 2 are his words; the narrator speaks from என்றலும். He defers the matter (நின் திறம் பின் அறிவாம்) and keeps to the sermon.
88.event: The sage hints that her kin are among the demon gods; Neelakesi is stricken, he puts the matter off and bids her hear dharma, and she agrees.

claims.claim: the Vyantara gods are of eight kinds

89.reading: The Jyotishka gods are also five, moon, sun, planets, constellations and stars; some circle Mount Mandara to the right, and others stand shining without moving.
89.nuance: The sun and moon are here gods of one class among many, ranked below the heaven-dwellers of 90, not supreme lights.

claims.claim: the luminary gods are five, some circling the world mountain and some fixed

90.reading: The sixteen Kalpa heavens run from Saudharma to Arana and Acyuta, and above them, take it, dwell the Vaimanikas in groups of three threes, nine and five.
90.nuance: The verse gives the count of the heavens as plain fact to a listener who is told to take it (கொள் நீ); line 2 of the edition carries a stray bracketed syllable.

claims.claim: there are sixteen Kalpa heavens and above them further heavens in groups of nine, nine and five

91.reading: Now the sage will tell a little of the great, hard-to-bear suffering of the hell-beings, who are the worst in this round of births.
91.nuance: The metre changes here to short lines for the account of hell, which runs to 101. The sage promises only 'a little' (சிறிது).

claims.claim: the hell-beings are the worst of all births and their suffering is hard to bear

92.reading: The hell-beings of the dark hells are five hundred bows in stature and are beings of pain that spreads over yojanas.
92.nuance: ஈரிருள் and the third line are hard to construe; the size of five hundred bows seems to be that of the beings of the lowest hell.

claims.claim: hell-beings have bodies of vast measure, five hundred bows tall

93.reading: Their black bodies, though cut into many pieces by sword-edges, join again like water.
93.nuance: The body that rejoins like water is what makes the pain without end: in hell even dismemberment is not an exit.

claims.claim: bodies in hell cut by blades rejoin like water

94.reading: Even when strong ones do violence to them, their bodies cannot be killed, and there are many such torments that cannot be told.

claims.claim: the bodies of hell-beings cannot be killed before their time

95.reading: Seeing their enemies of old, their eyes turn to embers, and they rush on and do great violence beyond counting.
95.nuance: The torment here comes from the hell-beings themselves, carrying their old enmity into hell, not from a judge. The first word was repaired from an old encoding; வேரியர் is read as enemies (வைரியர்).

claims.claim: old enemies meet in hell and wound each other without end

96.reading: They are neuter, and since pain runs through them greatly, no pleasure of union comes to them.
96.nuance: பேடி (neuter) fits the Jain teaching that hell-beings have no sex; lines 3 and 4 are obscure.

claims.claim: hell-beings are neuter and know no pleasure of union

97.reading: Naming 'the sin of killing' and 'the sin of eating flesh', the tormentors make the hell-beings go into fire and burn, and make them stand inside its mouth and cry out.
97.nuance: The verse names eating flesh as a sin separate from killing, so one who eats meat he did not kill is not cleared; this is the charge Neelakesi will open the Kundalakesi debate with (163). The tormentors (ஆக்குவார்) are not named, and the verse names no judge. வாயினுள் may be the mouth of the fire or of the hell.

claims.claim: killing is a sin punished by burning in hell
eating flesh is a sin of its own, punished in hell like killing

98.reading: When they long for water to drink, what comes to their eyes and what they can reach is nothing that can be thought pleasant.

claims.claim: hell-beings who thirst find nothing to relieve them

99.reading: Charred, bruised, burnt inside, boiling up, falling, crying, burning: for such great suffering there is no one who relieves them.
99.nuance: பரிபவரும் இல்லை (there is no one who takes pity or bears it for them) shuts out any rescuer: no god, kin or guru enters this hell.

claims.claim: no one relieves the suffering of the beings in hell

100.reading: There, in the hot fire, sinking, rising head over head, with smoke entering, they are gulped and swallowed and so suffer.

101.reading: Many beings a yojana in size, hard to bring to death, and burning fierce poison: no grace is food for those spoken of, the verse seems to say of hell's last torments.
101.nuance: The four short lines do not yield a clear sentence; அருளுணா may mean 'grace is not their food' or name a food of hell. The reading is a guess.

103.reading: After the poison-eating hell-beings in their birth without good, the sage turns to the pains of animals: frightened, each flees from another like the wind, and even standing still in confusion their minds are always afraid.
103.nuance: The metre changes again. The animal's pain is fear itself, which never leaves the mind, not torment by others.

claims.claim: animals live in constant fear of one another

links.note: In 64 the sage sees privately that the woman before him is a demon's daughter, not a princess; in 88 he lets it show in one word, நுமர் (your kin), among the demon class of the Vyantara gods.
links.teaches: The sage's knowledge of her true form, held silent in 64, becomes a tool of teaching: he names her kind inside a list of gods, so the cosmology itself unmasks her, and then defers it to keep her listening.

links.note: 83 denies that great penance raises the humans of the small islands; 86 says penance frees the humans of the land of deeds.
links.teaches: Penance is not a power that works anywhere: in this sermon its fruit depends on the land of one's birth, so the same act frees in one land and fails in another.

links.note: In 74 the sage promised to tell birth, its disease, and the medicine that cuts that disease; 86 names the medicine as penance that drives out the dark karma.
links.teaches: The promised medicine for birth turns out to be penance, and it is offered only to humans of the land of deeds, so the cure is narrower than the promise first sounded.

links.note: The sermon's hell names 'the sin of eating flesh' beside 'the sin of killing'; in 163 Neelakesi's first charge against the Buddha's way is that he does not call eating flesh a fault.
links.teaches: The hell scene supplies the doctrinal ground for the first debate: because eating is a sin apart from killing, a school that permits meat not killed by the eater stands accused before any metaphysics is argued.

links.note: Kural 255 says hell will not open its mouth to release the flesh-eater; Neelakesi 97 shows the flesh-eater burning inside the fire's mouth, crying out.
links.teaches: The couplet's closed mouth of hell, read beside the epic, becomes a place one is held and burned in, and the epic shows that the Kural's verdict falls on the eater as a sinner in his own right, not only on the killer.

gains.a: the epic's charge against eating flesh gains the Kural's warrant that eating, not only killing, keeps one in hell
gains.b: the couplet's bare image of a mouth that will not open gains a picture of what is suffered inside it

links.note: Tirumular puts in fire-mouthed hell those who said 'kill, stab'; the Neelakesi puts there those who ate the flesh as well as those who killed.
links.teaches: A Saiva and a Jain text each carry the guilt of a killing beyond the hand that strikes, one back to the man who ordered it and the other forward to the man who eats, so between them the whole chain around a death is held to account.

gains.a: the Jain charge against the eater is seen as one case of a wider rule of shared guilt that a Saiva text also holds
gains.b: Tirumular's extension of guilt to the speaker gains its counterpart in the consumer, which he leaves to his next verse on flesh

links.note: The Neelakesi's hell has no one to relieve the sufferer (பரிபவரும் இல்லையே); Arunagirinathar asks Murugan to come at speed when Death would drop him into the seven hells, so that his sins go.
links.teaches: The two answer opposite ways whether anyone can stand between a sinner's deeds and hell: the Jain sermon says no one can, the Murugan song asks that the god do exactly that; the conflict holds if பரிபவர் means one who relieves or rescues.

gains.a: the Jain hell's lack of a rescuer is seen as a stance against the hope of divine rescue that Tamil devotion voices
gains.b: the devotee's plea is seen against a doctrine for which such a plea has no one to hear it

links.note: Naladiyar 37 says the gains of human birth are many and should be used for the world beyond; Neelakesi 86 says only the humans of the land of deeds can reach bliss by penance.
links.teaches: The quatrain treats human birth as one opportunity, while the epic splits humanity by land and says the gain of release belongs only to those born where deeds and penance are possible.

gains.a: the epic's cosmological sorting of humans gains an ethical point: it matters where one is born because only there can the human gain be used
gains.b: the quatrain's general 'gains of human birth' gains a limit it does not state, that not every human birth carries them

new_concepts.gloss: the gods as a class of embodied beings in the round of births, ranked and numbered beside humans, animals and hell-beings

source_issues: Verse 102 is missing: the core file goes from 101 to 103, so the chapter has 23 verses for the span 80 to 103.
Verse 90, line 2 carries a stray bracketed syllable '(வோர்' at the end, apparently a variant or a misplaced fragment of line 3.
Verse 85, line 1 prints 'கோலமி னோன்றற்', where the sense seems to need கோலமில் தோன்றல்; line 3 prints 'தீண்டலு ரந்தரத்' for தீண்டலர் அந்தரத்.
Verse 95, line 1 was repaired from an old encoding (ேரி for ோ¢); 'வேரியர்' is read as enemies, but the original letter is not certain.
Verse 86, line 1: the name of the land of deeds (ஆவிதையம்) is unclear and may be corrupt.
